claim: Dopamine is released in the striatum during development.
source: Dopamine is released in the striatum during development and impacts the activity of Protein Kinase A (PKA) in striatal spiny projection neurons (SPNs).
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction regarding embryonic dopamine release.

claim: Dopamine impacts the activity of Protein Kinase A (PKA) in striatal spiny projection neurons (SPNs).
source: Dopamine is released in the striatum during development and impacts the activity of Protein Kinase A (PKA) in striatal spiny projection neurons (SPNs).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction about dopamine receptor signaling pathways.

claim: Systemic in vivo treatment with Gαs-coupled G-protein receptors (GPCRs) agonists enhanced excitatory synapses on direct pathway striatal spiny projection neurons (dSPNs).
source: Systemic in vivo treatment with Gαs-coupled G-protein receptors (GPCRs) agonists enhanced excitatory synapses on direct pathway striatal spiny projection neurons (dSPNs)
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G showing increased spine density and mEPSC frequency in dSPNs after SKF 81297 administration.

claim: Rapid production of excitatory synapses on indirect pathway neurons (iSPNs) required the activation of Gαs GPCRs in SPNs of both pathways.
source: whereas rapid production of excitatory synapses on indirect pathway neurons (iSPNs) required the activation of Gαs GPCRs in SPNs of both pathways.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1H showing that co-administration of Drd1 and A2a receptor agonists was necessary to increase synapses on iSPNs.

claim: In vitro Gαs activation was sufficient to enhance spinogenesis induced by glutamate photolysis in both dSPNs and iSPNs.
source: Nevertheless, in vitro Gαs activation was sufficient to enhance spinogenesis induced by glutamate photolysis in both dSPNs and iSPNs
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2 showing increased probability of spinogenesis with GPCR agonist treatment during glutamate uncaging.

claim: iSPNs in intact neural circuits have additional requirements for rapid synaptic development compared to in vitro conditions.
source: suggesting that iSPNs in intact neural circuits have additional requirements for rapid synaptic development.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference between in vivo requirements (both Drd1 and A2aR activation) and in vitro sufficiency (A2aR activation alone) for iSPN spinogenesis.

claim: Rapid synaptogenesis is promoted by the coordinated actions of glutamate and postsynaptic Gαs-coupled receptors.
source: We evaluated the in vivo effects of enhanced glutamate release from corticostriatal axons and postsynaptic PKA and discovered a mechanism of developmental plasticity wherein rapid synaptogenesis is promoted by the coordinated actions of glutamate and postsynaptic Gαs-coupled receptors.
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by multiple experimental approaches including pharmacogenetic, optogenetic, and glutamate uncaging experiments shown in Figures 2-5.

claim: Dopamine differentially regulates biochemical signaling, neuronal activity and synaptic plasticity in direct and indirect pathway striatal neurons.
source: Dopamine differentially regulates biochemical signaling (Nishi et al., 1999; 1997), neuronal activity and synaptic plasticity in these two classes of striatal neurons, promoting synaptic potentiation and depression through different receptor subtypes (Shen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The second postnatal week of life in mice is a period of rapid growth of excitatory synapses on SPNs.
source: In mice, the second postnatal week of life is a period of rapid growth of excitatory synapses on SPNs, a process driven by the release of glutamate from corticostriatal axons (Kozorovitskiy et al., 2012)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The balance of activity in direct and indirect pathway SPNs influences activity in the neocortex.
source: Furthermore, the balance of activity in direct and indirect pathway SPNs (dSPNs and iSPNs, respectively) influences activity in the neocortex, potentially altering the firing patterns of corticostriatal neurons via recurrent circuit interactions (Kozorovitskiy et al., 2012; Oldenburg and Sabatini, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In dSPNs, dopamine acts on type 1 dopamine receptor (Drd1), a Gαs-coupled GPCR to activate PKA.
source: In dSPNs, dopamine acts on type 1 dopamine receptor (Drd1), a Gαs-coupled GPCR to activate PKA, a critical enzyme involved in cell growth and plasticity (Nishi et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In iSPNs, dopamine activates type 2 dopamine receptors (Drd2), Gαi-coupled GPCRs, decreasing PKA activity.
source: In contrast, in iSPNs, dopamine activates type 2 dopamine receptors (Drd2), Gαi-coupled GPCRs, decreasing PKA activity.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about dopamine receptor signaling.

claim: PKA activity levels influence spinogenesis and synaptogenesis in cortical pyramidal neurons.
source: Since PKA activity levels influence spinogenesis and synaptogenesis in cortical pyramidal neurons (Kwon and Sabatini, 2011)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Embryonic striatum receives substantial dopaminergic innervation from substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) and the ventral tegmental area (VTA).
source: Dopamine is poised to regulate striatal signaling early in postnatal life, since embryonic striatum receives substantial dopaminergic innervation from substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) and the ventral tegmental area (VTA), as is evidenced by neuroanatomical studies (Hu et al., 2004) and direct functional assays showing embryonic dopamine release (Ferrari et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Dysfunctions of the dopaminergic system are linked to schizophrenia, obsessive compulsive disorder, and Tourette Syndrome.
source: First, dysfunctions of the dopaminergic system are linked to numerous diseases that are postulated to have a developmental origin, including schizophrenia (Lau et al., 2013; Laruelle, 2014), obsessive compulsive disorder (Nikolaus et al., 2010) and Tourette Syndrome (Buse et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Embryonic exposure to methamphetamine induces profound brain and behavioral abnormalities in offspring.
source: Second, embryonic exposure to drugs of abuse that act on the dopaminergic system, such as methamphetamine (Heller et al., 2001), induces profound brain and behavioral abnormalities in the offspring.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The dopamine transporter promoter is active in the neonatal striatum on postnatal day 1 (P1).
source: Consistent with early development of the dopaminergic projection from SNc/VTA to striatum, the dopamine transporter promoter is active and dopaminergic axons are found in the neonatal striatum on postnatal day 1 (P1)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A showing tdTomato expression driven by dopamine transporter gene promoter at P1.

claim: Dopaminergic axons are found in the neonatal striatum on postnatal day 1 (P1).
source: Consistent with early development of the dopaminergic projection from SNc/VTA to striatum, the dopamine transporter promoter is active and dopaminergic axons are found in the neonatal striatum on postnatal day 1 (P1)
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 1A showing densely innervating fibers within striatum at P1.

claim: At P10, tyrosine hydroxylase is expressed in SNc cell bodies and shows a punctate pattern in the striatum.
source: Figure 1B shows: At P10, immunohistochemistry for tyrosine hydroxylase shows expression in SNc cell bodies (left) and a punctate pattern in the striatum (right).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1B through immunohistochemistry data.

claim: The frequency of mEPSCs in Drd1 agonist exposed SPNs was 593 ± 168% of that in saline-treated controls.
source: The frequency of mEPSCs in Drd1 agonist exposed SPNs was 593 ± 168% of that in saline-treated controls (N = 7 and 8 neurons from 4 mice/group, Kruskal-Wallis test p = 0.0063, with p<0.05 for Dunn's multiple comparison post hoc test).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1G.

claim: mEPSC amplitude was not significantly different between control and Drd1 agonist groups in dSPNs.
source: mEPSC amplitude was 10.8 ± 1.6 and 12.7 ± 1.1 pA for control and Drd1 agonist groups and was not significantly different (one way ANOVA, p = 0.313).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Dendritic spine density in dSPNs was 0.29 ± 0.02 spines/µm for saline control and 0.60 ± 0.04 spines/µm for Drd1 agonist groups.
source: Dendritic spine density was 0.29 ± 0.02 spines/µm and 0.60 ± 0.04 spines/µm for saline control and Drd1 agonist groups respectively (p<0.001 on Dunnett's multiple comparison test after one-way ANOVA; N = 36 dendrites, 12 neurons from 3 mice and 21 dendrites in 7 neurons from 3 mice).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from imaging data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Pretreating mice with PKA antagonist H-89 prevented the effects of Drd1 agonist on mEPSC frequency and spine density in dSPNs.
source: Pretreating mice with a PKA antagonist H-89 (5 mg/kg) 30 min prior to agonist injection prevented the effects on mEPSC frequency and spine density
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1G showing no significant differences with H-89 pretreatment.

claim: Drd1 receptor activation alone is insufficient to increase synapse number in acute brain slices.
source: However, Drd1 receptor activation alone is insufficient to increase synapse number, as changes in mEPSC frequency or amplitude were not observed with incubation of acute brain slices in SKF 81297 in vitro (Figure 1—figure supplement 1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing no changes in mEPSC frequency or amplitude with in vitro Drd1 stimulation.

claim: dSPN excitatory synapse enhancement by Drd1 receptor agonist requires intact circuitry.
source: Thus, dSPN excitatory synapse enhancement by a single, acute dose of a Drd1 receptor agonist alone requires intact circuitry, as it cannot be induced in the slice.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference between in vivo effects (synapse enhancement) and in vitro effects (no enhancement) of Drd1 agonist.

claim: In vivo administration of SKF 81297 had no effects on excitatory synapses in iSPNs.
source: In contrast to the effects seen in dSPNs, in vivo administration of SKF 81297 had no effects on excitatory synapses in iSPNs (Figure 1H)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1H showing no significant changes in mEPSC frequency in iSPNs with Drd1 agonist alone.

claim: iSPNs express Gαs-coupled Adenosine 2a (A2a) receptor.
source: iSPNs express Gαs-coupled Adenosine 2a (A2a) receptor, which also enhances PKA activity (Higley and Sabatini 2010)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Administration of A2aR agonist CGS 21680 alone had no significant effect on iSPN dendritic spine density or mEPSC rate within 1 hr.
source: nevertheless, administration of an agonist of A2aRs (CGS 21680, 0.1 mg/kg) had no significant effect on iSPN dendritic spine density or mEPSC rate, within the rapid time-frame of 1 hr (140 ± 63% of control, p>0.05 for control vs. A2aR agonist post-hoc comparison; N = 11 neurons from 3 mice).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1H.

claim: Administering Drd2 receptor agonist quinpirole resulted in no significant differences from controls in iSPNs.
source: Similarly, administering an agonist of Gαi-coupled Drd2 receptors (quinpirole 0.5 mg/kg) also resulted in no significant differences from controls (132 ± 17.0% of control, p>0.05 for control vs. Drd2 agonist post hoc comparison; N = 8 neurons from 3 mice).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1H.

claim: Co-administration of Drd1 and A2a receptor agonists increased mEPSC frequency and dendritic spine density in iSPNs.
source: However, co-administration of Drd1 and A2a receptor agonists increased mEPSC frequency and dendritic spine density in iSPNs, with no change in mEPSC amplitude, suggesting an increase in the number of functional excitatory synapses (Figure 1H)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1H showing significant increases with combined agonist treatment.

claim: Drd1 activation increases dSPN excitability.
source: Since Drd1 activation also increases dSPN excitability, which in turn may increase recurrent corticostriatal glutamatergic transmission onto SPNs by altering cortical activity (Oldenburg and Sabatini, 2015)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Drd1 receptor activation induces locomotion in P8-13 pups.
source: Such stimulatory effects of dopamine on basal ganglia circuitry are consistent with the observation of Drd1 receptor activation-induced locomotion observed in pups, which normally show limited mobility at P8-13 (Dehorter et al., 2011; Wills et al., 2014) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Priming with Drd1 receptor agonist administration at P9 potentiated agonist-evoked locomotion at P11.
source: This acute locomotion induction has lasting consequences for behavior and brain development, since priming with Drd1 receptor agonist administration at P9 potentiated agonist-evoked locomotion at P11 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Focal photolysis of MNI-L-glutamate can trigger synaptogenesis in SPNs.
source: We directly tested this hypothesis ex vivo by examining the ability of exogenous glutamate exposure, through focal photolysis of MNI-L-glutamate, to trigger synaptogenesis in SPNs under different states of GPCR activation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Spatio-temporally controlled glutamate release can focally and rapidly induce de novo formation of a synapse-bearing dendritic spine on young cortical pyramidal neurons.
source: Spatio-temporally controlled glutamate release can focally and rapidly induce de novo formation of a synapse-bearing dendritic spine on young cortical pyramidal neurons
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with implicit reference to previous work.

claim: P8-13 SPNs of both pathways were capable of de novo spinogenesis in response to glutamate uncaging.
source: As was previously described for layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons, P8-13 SPNs of both pathways were capable of de novo spinogenesis in response to glutamate uncaging (Kozorovitskiy et al., 2012; Kwon and Sabatini, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and citations to previous work.

claim: The basal rate of spinogenesis for SPNs was similar to previously examined cortical neurons.
source: The basal rate of spinogenesis (the probability of induction of a structure shaped like a dendritic spine), as well as its dependence on uncaging pulse width and proximity to the dendrite were similar for striatal SPNs and previously examined cortical neurons (Kwon and Sabatini, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of current data in Figure 2 with cited previous work.

claim: The probability of spinogenesis increased in the presence of SKF 81297 for dSPNs.
source: The probability of spinogenesis increased in the presence of SKF 81297 for dSPNs, and CGS 21680 for iSPNs, respectively
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data in Figure 2D-E showing increased success rates with GPCR agonist treatment.

claim: The probability of spinogenesis increased in the presence of CGS 21680 for iSPNs.
source: The probability of spinogenesis increased in the presence of SKF 81297 for dSPNs, and CGS 21680 for iSPNs, respectively
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data in Figure 2D-E showing increased success rates with GPCR agonist treatment.

claim: Gαs-coupled receptor stimulation decreased the number of glutamate pulses necessary to induce spinogenesis.
source: Analysis of the time course of spine formation for successful inductions reveals that Gαs-coupled receptor stimulation decreased the number of glutamate pulses necessary to induce spinogenesis (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2F-G.

claim: Spine growth occurs rapidly in all conditions.
source: Whereas spine growth occurs rapidly in all conditions, as observed in pyramidal neurons (Kwon and Sabatini, 2011)
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2F and citation to previous work.

claim: SKF 81297 and CGS 21680 accelerated the onset of spinogenesis for dSPNs and iSPNs, respectively.
source: SKF 81297 and CGS 21680 accelerated the onset of spinogenesis for dSPNs and iSPNs, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis in Figure 2G showing reduced number of pulses to threshold.

claim: Cell-autonomous mechanisms exist for neuromodulatory regulation of glutamate-dependent spinogenesis.
source: Given that glutamate was exogenously controlled and Gαs receptors were stimulated by agonist bath application, these findings suggest the presence of cell-autonomous mechanisms for neuromodulatory regulation of glutamate-dependent spinogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental design where both glutamate and GPCR activation were externally controlled.

claim: Rs1 is a modified Gαs-coupled GPCR that can be activated by the small molecule RS 67333.
source: To test this prediction for PKA signaling, we used a pharmacogenetic approach based on Rs1, a modified Gαs-coupled GPCR that can be activated by the small molecule RS 67333
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by data in Figure 3A showing SEAP assay results.

claim: Rs1 activation by RS 67333 increases PKA activity in vitro.
source: Figure 3A shows: Secreted alkaline phosphatase (SEAP)-based in vitro test of the efficacy of PKA activation following activation of the Gαs-targeted RASSL with RS 67333.
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the SEAP assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Co-injection of Cre-expressing AAV and Cre-dependent AAV encoding Rs1 resulted in broad expression in dorsal striatum SPNs of both dSPNs and iSPNs.
source: This co-injection resulted in broad expression in dorsal striatum SPNs of the injected hemisphere in both dSPNs and iSPNs (Figure 3E) (0% vs. 98% co-labeling, N = 750 and 728 neurons in control and injected hemispheres, from 3 mice).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: There is a strong age dependence of peak amplitude of EPSCs in control conditions from P8 to P13/14.
source: In the control condition, there was a strong age dependence of peak amplitude of EPSCs, ranging from an average of 10 pA to an average of 196 pA per age group, in a cohort of P8-P13/14 mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Light-evoked EPSC amplitude was increased in virally transduced SPNs compared to control hemisphere SPNs.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, light-evoked EPSC amplitude was increased in virally transduced SPNs, compared to control hemisphere SPNs (Figure 3G; light-evoked EPSC amplitude, 68.6 ± 29.9 pA control vs. 150.3 ± 55.8 pA injected hemisphere; N = 21 and 23 neurons from 4 mice/group, t-test p = 0.039).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: In vivo transient activation of a Gαs-coupled GPCR in SPNs is sufficient to rapidly enhance corticostriatal connectivity.
source: Thus, in vivo transient activation of a Gαs-coupled GPCR in SPNs is sufficient to rapidly enhance corticostriatal connectivity, in the presence of otherwise normal corticostriatal transmission.
evidence: This is concluded from the pharmacogenetic experiment data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Concurrent pharmacogenetic activation of Gαs cascades in dSPNs enhances corticostriatal glutamatergic drive via recurrent connections.
source: The observed sufficiency of pharmacogenetic PKA activation to enhance corticostriatal connectivity for iSPNs (in contrast to stimulating iSPNs with an A2aR agonist, as in Figure 1H) stems from the likelihood that the concurrent pharmacogenetic activation of Gαs cascades in dSPNs enhances corticostriatal glutamatergic drive via recurrent connections and regulating cortical activity (Oldenburg and Sabatini, 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the difference in iSPN responses between A2aR agonist alone and pharmacogenetic activation of both pathways, supported by citation.

claim: In vivo optogenetic stimulation of Rbp4-Cre positive neurons in cortex increased c-fos expression on the stimulated side.
source: Figure 4B shows: Immunohistochemical labeling of immediate early gene c-fos product shows increased labeling on the optogenetically stimulated side.
evidence: This is directly shown by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 4B.

claim: In vivo optogenetic stimulation of corticostriatal afferents enhanced light-evoked EPSCs in SPNs.
source: Figure 4D shows successful induction of corticostriatal plasticity under baseline conditions with larger EPSC amplitudes on the stimulated side.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The functional reorganization induced through brief in vivo stimulation of corticostriatal afferents is locally expressed in the striatum.
source: These data demonstrate that a major component of the functional reorganization induced through brief in vivo stimulation of corticostriatal afferents in young mice is locally expressed in the striatum.
evidence: This is supported by data from striatum-only slice experiments shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Optogenetically-induced corticostriatal plasticity was blocked by pre-administration of PKA inhibitor H-89.
source: We further probed the pharmacological dependence of this form of plasticity and found that it was blocked by either pre-administration of PKA inhibitor H-89 (5 mg/kg)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4F showing no difference between control and stimulated hemispheres with H-89 treatment.

claim: Optogenetically-induced corticostriatal plasticity was blocked by a combination of Drd1 and A2aR blockers.
source: or by a combination of Drd1 and A2aR blockers SKF 83566 (0.5 mg/kg) and istradefylline/KW-6002 (2.5 mg/kg), administered 30 min before optogenetic stimulation (Figure 4F–G).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4G showing no difference between control and stimulated hemispheres with receptor blocker treatment.

claim: SPN changes induced by glutamatergic stimulation require PKA signaling.
source: Thus, SPN changes induced by glutamatergic stimulation require PKA signaling, which in turn is activated via Drd1 and A2aR for dSPNs and iSPNs, respectively.
evidence: This is concluded from the pharmacological blocking experiments shown in Figures 4F-G.

claim: Increasing either pre-synaptic glutamatergic drive or enhancing striatal PKA signaling is sufficient to rapidly alter SPN synaptogenesis.
source: Increasing either pre-synaptic glutamatergic drive or enhancing striatal PKA signaling is sufficient to rapidly alter SPN synaptogenesis, supporting the idea of cooperative, neuromodulation-dependent circuit remodeling during striatal development.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined results of pharmacogenetic (Figure 3) and optogenetic (Figure 4) experiments.

claim: Ex vivo optogenetic stimulation of corticostriatal afferents in the presence of drugs activating PKA in SPNs enhanced light-evoked EPSCs.
source: Figure 5D shows increased amplitudes of optogenetically evoked EPSCs in the stimulation condition compared to control.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: PKA activation and glutamate release within striatum are sufficient for strengthening corticostriatal synapses.
source: In order to directly evaluate whether PKA activation and glutamate release within striatum are sufficient for strengthening corticostriatal synapses, we performed ex vivo plasticity induction using optogenetic stimulation of corticostriatal afferents in the presence of drugs activating PKA in SPNs
evidence: This is supported by the ex vivo optogenetic stimulation experiment data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Neuromodulation, through the activity of PKA, enhances the probability of dendritic spine formation in the developing striatum.
source: Our data reveal that neuromodulation, through the activity of PKA, enhances the probability of dendritic spine formation and lowers the amount of glutamate necessary to trigger spinogenesis in the developing striatum.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by data from Figures 2-5.

claim: Neuromodulation lowers the amount of glutamate necessary to trigger spinogenesis in the developing striatum.
source: Our data reveal that neuromodulation, through the activity of PKA, enhances the probability of dendritic spine formation and lowers the amount of glutamate necessary to trigger spinogenesis in the developing striatum.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by data from Figure 2 showing reduced pulses to threshold with GPCR activation.

claim: dSPN activity is positively coupled to striatal glutamate release onto SPNs of both pathways through polysynaptic recurrent loops involving the neocortex.
source: Figure 6B shows: These results fit into the larger framework of the basal ganglia model, which indicates that through polysynaptic recurrent loops involving the neocortex, dSPN activity is positively coupled to striatal glutamate release onto SPNs of both pathways
evidence: This is stated as part of the basal ganglia circuit model and illustrated in Figure 6B.

claim: Indirect pathway activity provides negative feedback for striatal glutamate release.
source: whereas indirect pathway activity provides negative feedback.
evidence: This is stated as part of the basal ganglia circuit model shown in Figure 6B.

claim: During development, dSPNs have greater dendritic spine density compared to iSPNs.
source: During development, dSPNs have greater dendritic spine density and miniature EPSC frequency but not amplitude, compared to iSPNs. These graphs represent re-analyses of control data from a previously published study (Kozorovitskiy et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by re-analyzed data shown in Figure 6C from a previous publication.

claim: During development, dSPNs have greater miniature EPSC frequency compared to iSPNs.
source: During development, dSPNs have greater dendritic spine density and miniature EPSC frequency but not amplitude, compared to iSPNs.
evidence: This is supported by re-analyzed data shown in Figure 6C from a previous publication.

claim: During development, dSPNs and iSPNs do not differ in miniature EPSC amplitude.
source: During development, dSPNs have greater dendritic spine density and miniature EPSC frequency but not amplitude, compared to iSPNs.
evidence: This is supported by re-analyzed data shown in Figure 6C from a previous publication.

claim: PKA activity via Gαs GPCRs generally serves to potentiate activity-dependent synaptogenesis during the time of rapid synapse production.
source: The observation that two types of Gαs-dependent modulation appear to regulate synaptogenesis in d- and iSPNs raises the possibility that PKA activity, via Gαs GPCRs, generally serves to potentiate activity-dependent synaptogenesis during the time of rapid synapse production.
evidence: This is a speculative generalization based on the findings with Drd1 and A2aR.

claim: The array of Gαs GPCRs expressed in the central nervous system includes 5-HT4 and 5-HT7 serotonin receptors, beta-adrenergic receptors, and corticotropin-releasing factor receptors.
source: The array of Gαs GPCRs expressed in the central nervous system is substantial and includes abundant receptors such as 5-HT4 and 5-HT7 serotonin receptors (Giulietti et al., 2014), as well beta-adrenergic (Nomura et al., 2014; Arriza et al., 1992) and corticotropin-releasing factor receptors (Fu and Neugebauer, 2008; Riegel and Williams, 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: A general role for neuromodulators acting on Gαs GPCRs during neural circuit development would transform understanding of core principles in developmental neurobiology.
source: A general role for neuromodulators acting on Gαs GPCRs during neural circuit development would transform our understanding of core principles in developmental neurobiology, greatly expanding the list therapeutic targets for neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorders.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader implications of the findings.
